title: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS)
description: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is a chronic condition caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), first identified in the early 1980s.
subject: Pathophysiology
text: ACQUIRED IMMUNE DEFICIENCY SYNDROME (AIDS) Dr Ayesha Fatima Pharm D Assistant Professor Dept of Pharmacy Practice

INTRODUCTION 1. AIDS was first described in 1981 as a new disease. 2. In 1983, the causative agent was identified as Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). 3. HIV is a retrovirus. It is classified into: a. HIV-1 (most common and virulent) b. HIV-2 (less virulent, mainly in West Africa) 4. HIV primarily attacks CD4+ helper T cells. 5. Leads to: Progressive immune system destruction 6. Increased susceptibility to: Opportunistic infections, Malignancies 7. According to Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS: Approximately 34 million people are living with HIV/AIDS. 8. High prevalence regions: Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, South America 9. High-Risk Groups ▪ Individuals with: Multiple sexual partners , STIs ▪ Intravenous drug users ▪ Healthcare workers (occupational exposure) ▪ Infants born to HIV-positive mothers

Modes of Transmission HIV is transmitted through three main routes : Sexual Transmission 1. Most common mode. 2. Includes: Receptive anal intercourse , Vaginal intercourse 3. Risk increases with: Existing sexually transmitted infections (STIs): 1. Syphilis 2. Gonorrhea 3. Chlamydia 4. Herpes simplex 5. Trichomoniasis 6. Chancroid 4. Condom use reduces risk by ~20-fold Parenteral Transmission 1. Through exposure to infected blood: 1. Sharing needles (common in drug addicts) 2. Blood transfusion with infected blood 2. Healthcare workers: 1. Risk via needle-stick injuries Perinatal (Vertical) Transmission 1. From mother to child 2. Occurs: During pregnancy, At delivery, Through breastfeeding 3. Risk without treatment: Approximately 40% 4. Key factor: Maternal viral load at delivery

Morphologic Structure of HIV-1 1. Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 belongs to the lentivirus subgroup of retroviruses. 2. Diameter: ~100 nm 3. Shape: Spherical, enveloped virus 4. Surrounded by a lipoprotein envelope derived from host cell membrane

1. Envelope (Outer Layer): Lipid bilayer obtained from host cell during budding Contains 72 glycoprotein spikes Important proteins: 1. gp120 (surface glycoprotein) : Responsible for attachment (adhesion) to CD4 receptors on host cells. Loosely attached → easily shed into serum & lymphatic tissues 2. gp41 (transmembrane glycoprotein) : Anchors gp120 to viral envelope. Helps in fusion of virus with host cell membrane 3. May incorporate host proteins: HLA class I & II 4. Adhesion molecules like ICAM-1 2. Matrix Layer: Located just beneath the envelope, Composed of: p17 protein Functions: 1. Maintains viral structure 2. Anchors envelope to capsid 3. Capsid (Core) Cone-shaped central structure Made of: p24 protein (core antigen): p24 is an important diagnostic marker in early HIV infection 4. Nucleocapsid: Inside the capsid 1. Two copies of single-stranded RNA 2. RNA is associated with: p7 nucleoprotein

5. Viral Genome: Contains 2 identical strands of RNA . Carries genetic information required for replication 6. Enzymes (Essential for Replication) HIV contains enzymes necessary for its life cycle: 1. Reverse Transcriptase (p66) : Converts viral RNA → DNA 2. Integrase (p32) : Integrates viral DNA into host genome 3. Protease (p11) Cleaves viral proteins → maturation of virus 7. Additional Features 1. During budding, virus may carry host cell components 2. gp120 shedding contributes to: 1. Immune evasion 2. Circulating viral proteins in blood 1. gp120 → Attachment to CD4 cells 2. gp41 → Fusion with host membrane 3. p17 → Structural matrix protein 4. p24 → Core antigen (diagnostic marker) 5. p7 → RNA binding protein 6. RT, Integrase, Protease → Replication machinery

HIV Exposure ↓ Binding to CD4 T-cell (gp120 + CD4 receptor) ↓ Co-receptor Binding (CCR5 / CXCR4) ↓ Fusion with Host Cell (gp41 mediated) ↓ Release of Viral RNA + Enzymes into Cytoplasm ↓ Reverse Transcription (RNA → Double-stranded DNA by Reverse Transcriptase) ↓ Integration into Host Genome (by Integrase enzyme) ↓ Transcription & Translation (using host cell machinery) ↓ Formation of Immature Viral Particles ↓ Budding from Host Cell ↓ Maturation of Virus (Protease action) ↓ New Infectious Virions Released ↓ Infection of New CD4 Cells Pathophysiology

1. Cell may be destroyed due to: Direct viral damage ( cytolysis ) , Immune attack ( cytotoxic T-cells ) Natural cell death 2. Viral Distribution ~ 99% of HIV is present in: Lymph nodes, Immune-rich tissues 3. Acute Phase (Acute Retroviral Syndrome) : Often misdiagnosed or unnoticed Initial Infection ↓ Rapid Viral Replication (High Viremia) ↓ Drop in CD4 Cells ↓ Immune Response Begins (Antibody Production) ↓ Symptoms Appear: Fever Rash Lymphadenopathy Fatigue Night sweats

Viral Set Point Phase (Chronic Phase) ▪ Immune System Partially Controls Virus ↓ Balance Achieved: Virus Produced = Virus Destroyed ↓ Establishment of "Viral Set Point" ▪ Higher set point → Faster disease progression ▪ Lower set point → Slower progression

1. Primary (Acute) HIV Infection Common early symptoms (Acute Retroviral Syndrome): a. Fever b. Pharyngitis (sore throat) c. Lymphadenopathy (adenopathy) Other associated features: a. Rash b. Fatigue c. Night sweats Clinical Presentation

Disease Progression : Progression to AIDS depends on: Viral RNA load ▪ Higher viral load → Faster progression to AIDS Clinical Features in Children: Most HIV-infected children are asymptomatic initially Common physical findings: 1. Lymphadenopathy 2. Hepatomegaly 3. Splenomegaly 4. Failure to thrive 5. Weight loss / low birth weight 6. Fever of unknown origin

1. ELISA Test (Screening) Detects: Antibodies against HIV-1 , Highly sensitive and specific False Positive may occur in: Multiparous women , Recent infections: Hepatitis B , Influenza and After rabies vaccination False Negative : Early infection (window period) 2. Western Blot Assay 3. Viral Load Testing: Measures: Amount of HIV RNA (viremia) Methods: 1. RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase PCR) 2. Branched DNA assay 3. Nucleic acid sequence-based amplification 4. CD4 Count Normal range: 500 – 1600 cells/μL Important marker for: 1. Disease progression 2. Immune status Diagnosis
WHO Disease Staging System

1. General Principle HIV-infected individuals may remain asymptomatic when: CD4+ count is within normal range (500–1600 cells/μL) Goal: Maintain immune strength , Delay disease progression 2. Lifestyle Modifications a. Practice safe sexual behavior: Limit to one sexual partner , Consistent condom use b. Avoid exposure to infection: Do not share blades, razors, needles, or sharps c. Maintain personal hygiene: Regular handwashing, Clean surroundings 3. Dietary Measures Consume a nutritious, balanced diet, Well-cooked foods . Properly washed fruits and vegetables Avoid: Contaminated or raw foods (to prevent infections) Treatment Non-Pharmacological

4. Avoid Harmful Habits: Abstain from alcohol, Avoid smoking/tobacco , Avoid substance abuse 5. Infection Prevention Stay away from: Crowded or unhygienic environments and Situations increasing infection risk, Early management of minor infections 6. Overall Health Maintenance: Adequate rest and sleep, Regular physical activity (moderate), Stress management

▪ 1. Goal of Therapy Prevent viral replication ▪ Ultimate target: ▪ Undetectable viral load ▪ Benefits: ▪ Improves CD4+ count ▪ Reduces disease progression ▪ Prevents opportunistic infections ▪ 2. Guidelines ▪ Recommended by: ▪ International AIDS Society ▪ Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ▪ World Health Organization Treatment Pharmacological

Class Full Form Mechanism of Action Examples NRTIs Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors Inhibit reverse transcriptase enzyme and block conversion of RNA → DNA Zidovudine, Didanosine, Stavudine, Zalcitabine, Lamivudine, Abacavir NNRTIs Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors Directly inhibit reverse transcriptase enzyme ( non-competitive inhibition ) Nevirapine, Delavirdine, Efavirenz PIs Protease Inhibitors Inhibit protease enzyme and prevent formation of mature viral particles Saquinavir, Ritonavir, Indinavir, Nelfinavir, Amprenavir

About the Disease 1. HIV is a chronic manageable infection , not a death sentence 2. Caused by Human Immunodeficiency Virus which weakens the immune system 3. Progresses slowly if untreated → may lead to AIDS 4. Transmission occurs via: 1. Unprotected sexual contact 2. Blood and needle sharing 3. Mother-to-child transmission 5. Patients may remain asymptomatic for years Patient Education

About the Medication (ART) a) Antiretroviral therapy (ART): a) Controls viral replication b) Helps maintain/increase CD4 count b) Key counseling points: a) Strict adherence is essential (take medicines daily, same time) b) Missing doses → drug resistance & treatment failure c) Do not stop medication without consulting doctor d) Be aware of possible side effects and report them c) Goal: a) Achieve undetectable viral load

A. Prevention of Transmission ▪ Use condoms consistently ▪ Maintain single sexual partner ▪ Do not share: ▪ Needles ▪ Razors/blades B. Healthy Living ▪ Eat nutritious, well-cooked food ▪ Maintain personal hygiene ▪ Regular exercise and adequate rest D. Infection Prevention • Avoid: • Unhygienic environments • Contaminated food/water • Seek early treatment for infections E. Psychosocial Support • Maintain positive mental health • Seek family and social support • Avoid stigma and discrimination C. Avoid Harmful Habits • No alcohol • No smoking/tobacco • Avoid substance abuse 3. Lifestyle Modifications

Feature HIV Infection AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) Definition Infection caused by Human Immunodeficiency Virus Advanced stage of HIV infection Stage Early to chronic phase Final/advanced stage Immune Status CD4 count may be normal or mildly reduced Severely reduced CD4 (<200 cells/mm³) Symptoms Often asymptomatic or mild (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy) Severe symptoms due to opportunistic infections Opportunistic Infections Usually absent Common (TB, candidiasis, toxoplasmosis, etc.) Viral Load Variable, can be controlled with ART High if untreated Diagnosis HIV antibody/antigen tests (ELISA, etc.) HIV positive + AIDS-defining conditions Reversibility Can be controlled with ART Cannot be reversed, but can be managed Prognosis Good with treatment Poor if untreated

title: Disorders of digestive system
description: The document discusses various disorders of the digestive system, including oral conditions like thrush and gingivitis, as well as gastrointestinal issues such as peptic ulcers, inflammatory bowel disease, and acute pancreatitis. It outlines their causes, symptoms, complications, and underlying mechanisms, focusing on infections, inflammation, and anatomical abnormalities. Additionally, it highlights the importance of bacteria like Helicobacter pylori in gastrointestinal diseases and the role of environmental and genetic factors in conditions such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
subject: Pathophysiology
text:  By Dr. Ayesha Fatima Pharm D Assistant Professor Dept. of Pharmacy Practice DISORDERS OF DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Thrush (oral candidiasis) • This acute fungal infection of the epithelium of the mouth is caused by the yeast Candida albicans , which grows in white patches on the tongue and oral mucosa. • In adults it causes opportunistic infection mainly in debilitated people and in those whose immunity is lowered by, e.g., steroids, antibiotics or cytotoxic drugs. • In babies it may be a severe infection, sometimes causing epidemics in nurseries by cross-infection. It occurs most commonly in bottle-fed babies. • Chronic thrush may develop, affecting the roof of the mouth in people who wear dentures. The fungus survives in fine grooves on the upper surface of the denture and repeatedly reinfects the oral mucosa. Aphthous stomatitis (recurrent oral ulceration) • This common condition features extremely painful ulcers that occur singly or in crops inside the mouth. The cause is unknown.

Gingivitis This is inflammation of the gums, which may be acute or chronic. Acute gingivitis • This is a rare condition previously known as Vincent’s infection, in which there is severe • inflammation that mainly affects the gums. • It is caused by two commensal organisms acting together, Borrelia vincenti and a fusiform bacillus. • Both organisms may be present in the mouth but only cause the condition in the presence of malnutrition, debilitating disease, poor oral hygiene or injury caused by previous infection. Chronic gingivitis • This common inflammatory condition occurs in response to accumulation of bacterial plaque around the teeth. • It causes bleeding gums and gradually destroys the tissues that support the teeth, which eventually loosen and may fall out.

Acute oesophagitis • This arises after caustic materials are swallowed and also if immunocompromised people acquire severe fungal infections, typically candidiasis, or viral infections, e.g. Herpes simplex . • Dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing) is usually present. Following severe injury, healing causes fibrosis, and there is a risk of oesophageal stricture developing later, as the fibrous tissue shrinks. Reflux oesophagitis • This condition, the commonest cause of indigestion (or ‘ heartburn ’ ), is caused by persistent regurgitation of acidic gastric juice into the oesophagus, causing irritation, inflammation and painful ulceration. • Haemorrhage occurs when blood vessels are eroded. • Persistent reflux leads to chronic inflammation and if damage is extensive, secondary healing with fibrosis occurs. • Shrinkage of mature fibrous tissue may cause stricture of the oesophagus. • This condition sometimes gives rise to Barrett ’ s oesophagus. • Reflux of gastric contents is associated with: increase in the intra-abdominal pressure, e.g. in pregnancy, constipation and obesity high acid content of gastric juice low levels of secretion of the hormone gastrin, leading to reduced sphincter action at the lower end of the oesophagus the presence of hiatus hernia

Gastritis Inflammation of the stomach can be an acute or chronic condition. Acute gastritis • This is usually a response to irritant drugs or alcohol. • The drugs most commonly implicated are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) including aspirin, even at low doses. • Other causes include the initial response to Helicobacter pylori infection and severe physiological stress, e.g. in extensive burns and multiple organ failure. • Mild cases can be asymptomatic or may present with nausea and vomiting associated with inflammatory changes of the gastric mucosa. • Erosions can also occur, which are characterized by tissue loss affecting the superficial layers of the gastric mucosa. • In more serious cases, there are multiple erosions, which may result in life-threatening haemorrhage causing haematemesis (vomiting of frank blood or black ‘ coffee grounds ’ when there has been time for digestion of blood to occur) and melaena (passing black tarry faeces), especially in elderly people. Where there has been extensive tissue damage, healing is by fibrosis causing reduced elasticity and peristalsis.

Chronic gastritis • Chronic gastritis is a milder longer-lasting condition. It is usually associated with Helicobacter • pylori but is sometimes due to autoimmune disease or chemical injury. It is more common in later life. Helicobacter -associated gastritis • The microbe Helicobacter pylori can survive in the gastric mucosa and is commonly associated with gastric conditions, especially chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Peptic ulceration • Ulceration involves the full thickness of the gastrointestinal mucosa. • It is caused by disruption of the normal balance between the corrosive effect of gastric juice and the protective effect of mucus on the gastric epithelial cells. • The most common sites for ulcers are the stomach and the first few centimetres of the duodenum. • More rarely they occur in the oesophagus and round the anastomosis of the stomach and small intestine, following gastrectomy. • The underlying causes are not known but, if gastric mucosal protection is impaired, the epithelium can be exposed to gastric acid causing the initial cell damage that leads to ulceration. • The main protective mechanisms are: 1. good blood supply, 2. adequate mucus secretion and 3. efficient epithelial cell replacement.

Blood supply • Reduced blood flow and ischaemia may be caused by excessive cigarette smoking and severe stress, either physical or mental. • In stressful situations the accompanying sympathetic activity causes constriction of the blood vessels supplying the alimentary tract. Secretion of mucus • The composition and the amount of mucus may be altered, e.g.: by regular and prolonged use of aspirin and other anti-inflammatory drugs by the reflux of bile acids and salts in chronic gastritis. Epithelial cell replacement • There is normally a rapid turnover of gastric and intestinal epithelial cells. • This may be reduced: by raised levels of steroid hormones, e.g. in response to stress or when they are used as drugs in chronic gastritis by irradiation and the use of cytotoxic drugs. • In peptic ulcer disease, the alimentary tract is commonly colonised by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori , a causative agent in this disorder.

Acute peptic ulcers • These lesions involve tissue to the depth of the submucosa and may be single or multiple. • They are found in many sites in the stomach and in the first few centimetres of the duodenum. • Their development is often associated with acute gastritis, severe stress, e.g. severe illness, shock, burns, severe emotional disturbance and following surgery. • Healing without the formation of fibrous tissue usually occurs when the stressor is removed, although haemorrhage, which may be life- threatening, can be a complication.

Chronic peptic ulcers • These ulcers penetrate through the epithelial and muscle layers of the stomach wall and may include the adjacent pancreas or liver. • In the majority of cases they occur singly in the pylorus of the stomach and in the duodenum. Occasionally there are two ulcers facing each other in the duodenum, called kissing ulcers. Helicobacter pylori is found in 90% of people with duodenal ulcers and 70% of those with gastric ulcers. • The remaining gastric ulcers are almost entirely due to non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Smoking predisposes to peptic ulceration and delays healing. • Healing occurs with the formation of fibrous tissue and subsequent shrinkage may cause: stricture of the lumen of the stomach gastric outflow obstruction or stenosis of the pyloric sphincter adhesions to adjacent structures, e.g. pancreas, liver, transverse colon.

Complications of peptic ulcers 1. Haemorrhage a. When a major artery is eroded a serious and possibly life-threatening haemorrhage may occur, causing shock, haematemesis and/or melaena. 2. Anaemia a. Chronic persistent low level bleeding from an ulcer may lead to development of iron deficiency anaemia. 3. Perforation a) When an ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the wall of the stomach or duodenum their contents enter the peritoneal cavity, causing acute peritonitis. b) Infected inflammatory material may collect under the diaphragm, forming a subphrenic abscess and the infection may spread through the diaphragm to the pleural cavity. 1. Gastric outflow obstruction a. Also known as pyloric stenosis , fibrous tissue formed as an ulcer in the pyloric region heals, causes narrowing of the pylorus that obstructs outflow from the stomach and results in persistent vomiting. 2. Development of a malignant tumour a. This is frequently associated with chronic gastritis caused by Helicobacter pylori .

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) • This term includes Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. • Their aetiology is unknown but is thought to involve environmental and immune factors in genetically susceptible individuals. Both conditions typically have a pattern of relapse and remission.

Crohn ’ s disease • This chronic inflammatory condition of the alimentary tract, also known as regional ileitis, usually occurs in young adults. • The terminal ileum and the rectum are most commonly affected but the disease may affect any part of the tract. • There is chronic patchy inflammation with oedema of the full thickness of the intestinal wall, causing partial obstruction of the lumen, sometimes described as skip lesions . • There are periods of remission of varying duration. • The main symptoms are diarrhoea, abdominal pain and weight loss. • Complications include: • secondary infections, occurring when inflamed areas ulcerate fibrous adhesions and subsequent intestinal obstruction caused by the healing process fistulae between intestinal lesions and adjacent structures, e.g. loops of bowel, • surface of the skin perianal fistulae, • fissures and skin tags cancer of the small or large intestine.

Ulcerative colitis • This is a chronic inflammatory disease of the mucosa of the colon and rectum, which may ulcerate and become infected. • It usually occurs in young adults and begins in the rectum and sigmoid colon. • From there it may spread proximally to involve a variable proportion of the colon and, sometimes, the entire colon. • The main symptom is bloody diarrhoea. There are periods of remission lasting weeks, months or years. Individuals may develop other systemic problems affecting, for example, the joints (ankylosing spondylitis, skin and liver. • In long-standing cases, cancer sometimes develops. • Toxic megacolon is an acute complication where the colon loses its muscle tone and dilates. • There is a high risk of electrolyte imbalance, perforation and hypovolaemic shock, which may be fatal if untreated.

Hernias • A hernia is a protrusion of an organ or part of an organ through a weak point or aperture in the surrounding structures. • In those affecting the digestive system, a piece of bowel protrudes through a weak point in either the musculature of the anterior abdominal wall or an existing opening. • It occurs when there are intermittent increases in intra-abdominal pressure, most commonly in men who lift heavy loads at work. • The underlying causes of the abdominal wall weakness are unknown. • Outcomes include: spontaneous reduction, i.e. the loop of bowel slips back to its correct place when the intra-abdominal pressure returns to normal manual reduction, i.e. by applying gentle pressure over the abdominal swelling strangulation , when reduction is not possible and the venous drainage from the herniated loop of bowel is obstructed, causing congestion, ischaemia and gangrene. • In addition there is intestinal obstruction.

Sites of hernias 1. Inguinal hernia 1. The weak point is the inguinal canal, which contains the spermatic cord in the male and the round ligament in the female. 2. It occurs more commonly in males than in females. 2. Femoral hernia 1. The weak point is the femoral canal through which the femoral artery, vein and lymph vessels pass from the pelvis to the thigh. 3. Umbilical hernia 1. The weak point is the umbilicus where the umbilical blood vessels from the placenta entered the fetus before birth. 4. Incisional hernia 1. This is caused by repeated stretching of fibrous tissue formed after previous abdominal surgery.

5. Hiatus hernia a. This is the protrusion of a part of the fundus of the stomach through the oesophageal opening in the diaphragm . Although often asymptomatic, irritation of the oesophagus only occurs when there is reflux of acid gastric juice, especially when the individual lies flat or bends down. b. The long term effects may be oesophagitis, fibrosis and narrowing of the oesophagus, causing dysphagia. Strangulation does not occur. 6. Rolling hiatus hernia a. An abnormally large opening in the diaphragm allows a pouch of stomach to ‘roll’ upwards into the thorax beside the oesophagus. b. This is associated with obesity and increased intra-abdominal pressure. 7. Sliding hiatus hernia a. Part of the stomach is pulled upwards into the thorax. The abnormality may be caused by shrinkage of fibrous tissue formed during healing of a previous oesophageal injury. b. The sliding movement of the stomach in the oesophageal opening is due to shortening of the oesophagus by muscular contraction during swallowing.

8. Peritoneal hernia a. A loop of bowel may herniate through the epiploic foramen, the opening in the lesser omentum that separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs. 9. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia a. Incomplete formation of the diaphragm, usually on the left side, allows abdominal organs such as the stomach and loops of intestine into the thoracic cavity, preventing normal development of the fetal lungs.

Acute pancreatitis • Proteolytic enzymes produced by the pancreas are secreted in inactive forms, which are not activated until they reach the intestine; this protects the pancreas from digestion by its own enzymes. • If these precursor enzymes are activated while still in the pancreas, pancreatitis results. • The severity of the disease is directly related to the amount of pancreatic tissue destroyed. • Mild forms are more common and damage only those cells near the ducts. Recovery is usually complete. • Severe forms cause widespread damage with necrosis and haemorrhage. • Common complications include infection, suppuration, and local venous thrombosis. Pancreatic enzymes, especially amylase, enter and circulate in the blood, causing similar damage to other structures. In severe cases there is a high mortality rate. • The causes of acute pancreatitis are not clear but known predisposing factors are gallstones and • alcoholism. • Other associated conditions include: cancer of the ampulla or head of pancreas viral infections, notably mumps kidney and liver transplantation hyperparathyroidism severe hypothermia drugs, e.g. corticosteroids, some cytotoxic agents.

Chronic pancreatitis • This is either due to repeated attacks of acute pancreatitis or may arise gradually without evidence of pancreatic disease. • It is more common in men and is frequently associated with fibrosis and distortion of the main pancreatic duct. • There is intestinal malabsorption when pancreatic secretions are reduced and diabetes mellitus occurs when severe damage affects the β-islet cells. • Protein material secreted by the acinar cells blocks the tiny acinar ducts. • This eventually leads to the formation of encapsulated cysts which are a feature of acute and chronic pancreatitis. • The most common cause in the Western world is excessive chronic alcohol consumption. • In developing countries dietary factors and malnutrition have been implicated. It is also associated with cystic fibrosis.

Acute hepatitis • Areas of necrosis develop as groups of hepatocytes die and the eventual outcome depends on the size and number of these areas. • Causes of the damage may be a variety of conditions, including: viral infections toxic substances circulatory disturbances. Viral hepatitis • Viral infections are the commonest cause of acute liver injury and different types are recognised. • The types are distinguished serologically, i.e. by the antibodies produced to combat the infection. • The severity of the ensuing disease caused by the different virus types varies considerably, but the pattern is similar. The viruses enter the liver cells, causing degenerative changes.

• An inflammatory reaction ensues, accompanied by production of an exudate containing lymphocytes, plasma cells and granulocytes. • There is reactive hyperplasia of the hepatic macrophages (Kupffer cells) in the walls of the sinusoids. • As groups of cells die, necrotic areas of varying sizes develop, phagocytes remove the necrotic material and the lobules collapse. • The basic lobule framework becomes distorted and blood vessels develop kinks. These changes interfere with the circulation of blood to the remaining hepatocytes and the resultant hypoxia causes further damage. • Fibrous tissue develops in the damaged area, and adjacent hepatocytes proliferate. The effect of these changes on the overall functioning of the liver depends on the size of the necrotic areas, the amount of fibrous tissue formed and the extent to which the blood and bile channels are distorted.

Hepatitis A • Previously known as ‘ infectious hepatitis ’ , this type affects mainly children, causing a mild illness. • Infection is spread by hands, food, water and fomites contaminated by infected faeces. • The incubation period is 15 to 40 days and the viruses are excreted in the faeces for 7 to 14 days before clinical symptoms appear and for about 7 days after. • Symptoms may include general malaise followed by a period of jaundice , that is accompanied by passing of dark urine and pale faeces. • Antibodies develop and confer lifelong immunity after recovery. Subclinical disease may occur but not carriers.

Hepatitis B • Previously known as ‘ serum hepatitis ’ , infection occurs at any age, but mostly in adults. • The incubation period is 50 to 180 days. • The virus enters the blood and is spread by blood and blood products. • People at greatest risk of infection are those who come in contact with blood and blood products in the course of their work, e.g. health-care workers. • The virus is also spread by body fluids, i.e. saliva, semen, vaginal secretions, and from mother to fetus (vertical transmission). • Others at risk include IV drug users and men who have sex with men.

Hepatitis C • This virus is spread by blood and blood products, which accounts for the infection of many people with haemophilia. • It is prevalent in IV drug users. • The infection is very frequently asymptomatic as a carrier state occurs. • Infection is usually diagnosed later in life when cirrhosis (see opposite) or chronic liver failure becomes evident. • Antibodies are formed and immunity persists after recovery. Infection usually leads to severe illness lasting 2 to 6 weeks, often followed by a protracted convalescence. • Carriers may, or may not, have had clinical disease. • Type B virus may cause massive liver necrosis and death. In less severe cases recovery may be complete. In chronic hepatitis (see opposite) that may develop, live viruses continue to circulate in the blood and other body fluids. • The condition is thought to predispose to liver cancer.

Gallstones (cholelithiasis) • Gallstones consist of deposits of the constituents of bile, most commonly cholesterol. Many small stones or one or more large stones may form but they do not necessarily produce symptoms. • Predisposing factors include: • changes in the composition of bile that affect the solubility of its constituents high blood cholesterol levels • diabetes mellitus • female gender • obesity • several pregnancies in young women, especially when accompanied by obesity.

Acute cholecystitis • This is acute inflammation of the gall bladder usually associated with gallstones, and occurs when a gallstone becomes impacted (stuck) in the cystic duct, often after a fatty meal. • Strong peristaltic contractions of the smooth muscle in the wall of the cystic duct that occur in an attempt to move the stone onwards result in biliary colic , severe acute pain in the right hypochondrium. • This does not cause jaundice because bile from the liver can still pass directly into the duodenum. Bile is unable to leave the gall bladder and an inflammatory reaction follows. • This may be complicated by bacterial infection and distension of the gall bladder, which carries the risk of perforation and peritonitis.

Chronic cholecystitis • The onset is usually insidious, sometimes following repeated acute attacks. • Gallstones are invariably present and there may be accompanying biliary colic. • Pain is due to the spasmodic contraction of muscle, causing ischaemia when the gall bladder is packed with gallstones. • There is usually secondary infection with suppuration. • Ulceration of the tissues between the gall bladder and the duodenum or colon may occur with fistula formation and, later, fibrous adhesions.

Jaundice • This is not a disease in itself, but yellowing of the skin and mucous membrane is a sign of abnormal bilirubin metabolism and excretion. Bilirubin, produced from the breakdown of haemoglobin, is normally conjugated in the liver and excreted in the bile. • Conjugation, the process of adding certain groups to the bilirubin molecule, makes it water-soluble and greatly enhances its removal from the blood, an essential step in excretion. • Unconjugated bilirubin, which is fat-soluble, has a toxic effect on brain cells. However, it is unable to cross the blood – brain barrier until the plasma level rises above 340 μmol/l, but when it does it may cause neurological damage, seizures (fits) and mental impairment. • Serum bilirubin may rise to 40 to 50 μmol/l before the yellow coloration of jaundice is evident in the skin and conjunctiva (normal 3 to 13 μmol/l). Jaundice is often accompanied by pruritus (itching) caused by the irritating effects of bile salts on the skin. • Jaundice develops when there is an abnormality of bilirubin processing.

Types of jaundice Whatever stage in bilirubin processing is affected, the end result is rising blood bilirubin levels. 1. Pre-hepatic jaundice • This is due to increased haemolysis of red blood cells that results in • production of excess bilirubin. Because the excess bilirubin is unconjugated it cannot be excreted in the urine, which therefore remains normal in colour. • Neonatal haemolytic jaundice occurs in many babies, especially in those born prematurely where the normal high haemolysis is coupled with shortage of conjugating enzymes in the hepatocytes of the still immature liver.

2. Intra-hepatic jaundice • This is the result of damage to the liver itself by, e.g.: viral hepatitis • toxic substances, such as drugs amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery) cirrhosis. • Excess bilirubin accumulates in the liver. Because it is mainly in the conjugated form, it is • water-soluble and excreted in the urine making it dark in colour. 3. Post-hepatic jaundice • Causes of obstruction to the flow of bile in the biliary tract include: gallstones in the common bile duct tumour of the head of the pancreas • fibrosis of the bile ducts, following cholangitis or injury by the passage of gallstones. • In this situation excess bilirubin is also conjugated and is therefore excreted in the urine. • The effects of raised serum bilirubin include: pruritus (itching) pale faeces due to absence of stercobilin dark urine due to the presence of increased amounts of bilirubin.
THANK YOU

title: Family Planning - Role of Pharmacist in Family Planning
description: Role of Pharmacist in Family Planning
subject: Community Pharmacy
text: FAMILY PLANNING ROLE OF PHARMACIST IN FAMILY PLANNING Family planning is often used as a synonym for birth control and usually applied to the circumstance of couples who wish to space between the children they want to have. Family planning is a technique that delays the pregnancy rather than preventing the pregnancy entirely. WHO defines 'family planning as a way of living and thinking that is adopted voluntarily upon the basis of knowledge, attitudes and responsible decisions of individuals and couples in order to promote the health and welfare of the family group and thus contributes effectively to the social development of a country. WHO has appreciated the role of pharmacists in educating the patients' about advantages of family planning and useful techniques the couple can adopt suiting to their family conditions. OBJECTIVES OF FAMILY PLANNING 1. To avoid unwanted births 2. To bring about wanted births 3. To regulate intervals between the pregnancies 4. To determine the number of children in the family 5. To control pregnancies in relation to the age of the parent 6. To prevent the frequent pregnancies induced stress on the physical and psychological health of the mother. ROLE OF PHARMACIST IN FAMILY PLANNING The pharmacist serves as an important link between the public and healthcare providers. Therefore, pharmacists often encounter individuals with diverse beliefs and misconceptions about family planning. Illiterate or less-educated populations may not be aware of the

dangerous, or harmful to health. The pharmacist plays a vital role in dispelling these fears and promoting awareness. 1. Health Education: Displays posters and distributes pamphlets to create awareness about family planning and small family norms. 2. Public Awareness Programs: Conducts health education campaigns and highlights the consequences of overpopulation. 3. Patient Counseling: Advises individuals and couples on the importance of family planning and spacing between children. 4. Addressing Myths: Provides counseling to remove misconceptions, fears, and cultural barriers related to contraception. 5. Contraceptive Guidance: Helps in selecting appropriate contraceptive methods based on patient needs and health status. 6. Drug Information: Explains the use, benefits, and side effects of oral contraceptives and other methods. 7. Promotion of Barrier Methods: Encourages use of condoms for dual protection (pregnancy prevention + STDs). 8. Dispensing Role: Ensures proper dispensing and storage of contraceptive products and improves accessibility. 9. Emergency Contraception: Provides timely guidance and access to emergency contraceptive methods. 10. Referral Services: Refers patients to doctors or family planning clinics for procedures like IUD insertion or sterilization. 11. Public Health Participation: Participates in national family planning programs and promotes reproductive health awareness.

12. Monitoring & Safety: Monitors adverse effects of contraceptives and stays updated with latest guidelines. CONTRACEPTIVE METHODS An ideal contraceptive method should be safe, effective, acceptable, easy to use, and economical. CLASSIFICATION OF CONTRACEPTIVE METHODS A. Temporary Methods (Spacing Methods) 1. Barrier Methods 1. Physical Methods a. Male condom b. Diaphragm c. Vaginal sponge 2. Chemical Methods (Spermicides) a. Foams b. Creams c. Pastes d. Jellies e. Suppositories f. Soluble films 3. Combined Methods a. Physical + Chemical methods 2. Intrauterine Devices (IUDs) 1. First-Generation (Non-medicated) a. Lippes Loop b. Loops, spirals, coils, rings 2. Second-Generation (Copper-containing) a. Copper-T 200 b. Copper-7 c. Nova-T d. Multiload 3. Third-Generation (Hormone-releasing) a. Progestasert 3. Hormonal Contraceptives

1. Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) 2. Progesterone-only pills (POPs) 3. Postcoital (emergency) pills 4. Once-a-month pills 5. Male pills 6. Depot formulations a. Injectable contraceptives (DMPA, NET-EN) b. Subdermal implants (Norplant) 7. Vaginal rings 4. Post-Conceptional Methods 1. Menstrual regulation 2. Menstrual induction 5. Miscellaneous Methods 1. Behavioral Methods a. Abstinence b. Coitus interruptus (withdrawal method) c. Safe period method 2. Natural Methods a. Basal body temperature method b. Cervical mucus method B. Permanent Methods (Sterilization) 1. Male Sterilization a. Vasectomy 2. Female Sterilization a. Tubectomy i. Laparoscopy ii. Mini-laparotomy TEMPORARY METHODS 1. Barrier Methods Barrier methods are available for both males and females. Their mechanism of action is to prevent the union of sperm and ovum, either mechanically or chemically. Physical Methods: These include condoms, diaphragms, and vaginal sponges. 1. Male Condom : A male condom is a contraceptive device made of latex. Some condoms are coated with a lubricant or spermicide. They are available in different sizes, shapes, colors, and textures. The condom is worn over the erect penis.

Precautions 1. Ensure it is free from tears and leaks 2. Discard after single use Advantages 1. Inexpensive 2. Safe 3. Easy to use and reliable 4. Provides protection against STDs and AIDS 5. No systemic side effects 6. Lightweight, compact, and easily disposable 7. Can be used by men of all age Disadvantages 1. Latex or lubricants may cause allergic reactions in some individuals 2. Incorrect use may lead to slipping or tearing during intercourse 3. Some men feel it reduces sexual pleasure Diaphragm A diaphragm is a vaginal barrier device made of synthetic rubber or plastic with a flexible spring ring. It is inserted into the vagina before intercourse. Precautions 1. Must remain in place for at least 6 hours after intercourse Advantages 1. No systemic risks 2. No major medical contraindications Disadvantages 1. Requires initial guidance from a trained person for proper insertion 2. Privacy is needed for insertion 3. Prolonged use may lead to toxic shock syndrome Vaginal Sponge It is a small polyurethane sponge saturated with a spermicidal agent (e.g., nonoxynol-9). It is inserted into the vagina just before intercourse. Disadvantages Less effective compared to the diaphragm Chemical Method s: These methods use spermicidal agents, available as: 1. Foams 2. Creams, pastes, and jellies 3. Suppositories 4. Soluble film

Mechanism of Action : These preparations contain surface-active agents that attach to spermatozoa, inhibit oxygen uptake, and destroy the sperms. Advantages 1. Safe 2. Woman-controlled methods 3. Provide some protection against sexually transmitted diseases Disadvantages 1. Higher failure rate when used alone 2. May cause mild irritation, burning, or discomfort 3. Must be used immediately before intercourse Combined Methods: Physical and chemical methods, when used alone, may have higher failure rates. Therefore, they can be used together as combined methods to improve effectiveness. 2. Intrauterine Devices (IUDs): An intrauterine device (IUD) is usually a small, flexible plastic frame that is inserted into the uterus to prevent pregnancy. Types of IUDs 1. First-Generation IUDs: These are non-medicated (inert) devices made of polyethylene. They are available in various sizes and shapes such as loops, spirals, coils, and rings. The Lippes Loop is a commonly used device, which is S-shaped. Advantages 1. Simple and easy to insert 2. Economical 3. Reversible method 4. Does not interfere with sexual pleasure Disadvantages 1. Requires a trained person for insertion 2. Needs regular follow-up 3. Requires periodic replacement 4. Rarely, it may be associated with complications such as uterine irritation 2. Second-Generation IUDs These are copper-containing devices. Older devices include Copper-7 and Copper-T 200, while newer ones include Nova-T and Multiload devices. Advantages 1. Low

2. Reduced incidence of side effects such as pain and bleeding 3. Easier to insert, even in nulliparous women 4. Increased contraceptive efficacy due to the presence of copper 3. Third-Generation IUDs These are hormone-releasing devices. The commonly used device is Progestasert, which is a T-shaped device containing progesterone. It releases approximately 65 micrograms of hormone per day into the uterus. Mechanism of Action 1. Thickens cervical mucus 2. Inhibits endometrial growth 3. Prevents fertilization and implantation 3. Hormonal Contraceptives Hormonal contraceptives are among the most effective spacing methods of contraception. They can be administered orally, as injections, implants, or vaginal devices. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) contain two hormones similar to those naturally present in a woman’s body: estrogen and progestin. Some contraceptives contain both hormones, while others contain progestin only. These are commonly referred to as combined pills, oral contraceptives (OCs), or birth control pills. Mechanism of Action Inhibit ovulation (prevent release of the ovum) Thicken cervical mucus, making sperm penetration difficult Do not disrupt an existing p Classification of Hormonal Contraceptives 1. Combined oral contraceptive pills 2. Progesterone-only pills 3. Postcoital (emergency) pills 4. Once-a-month pills 5. Male pills 6. Depot formulations 7. Injectable contraceptives 8. Subdermal implants 9. Vaginal rings

(a) Combined Oral Contraceptive (COC) Pills These contain 30–35 mcg of synthetic estrogen and 0.1–1 mg of progesterone. One pill is taken daily for 21 days, starting from the 5th day of the menstrual cycle. Not recommended for breastfeeding women, as they may reduce the quality and quantity of breast milk. Examples: Mala-N, Mala-D Risks and Precautions 1. Long-term use may increase the risk of: 2. Stroke 3. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 4. Myocardial infarction 5. Higher risk in: 6. Women >35 years 7. Smokers 8. Patients with hypertensio (b) Progesterone-Only Pills (POPs) These contain small amounts of progestin only and no estrogen. They are also called mini-pills. Features 1. Contain lower hormone doses compared to COCs 2. Suitable for breastfeeding women 3. Do not interfere with milk production 4. Do not disrupt an existing pregnancy (c) Emergency (Postcoital) Pills These are used after unprotected intercourse to prevent pregnancy and are also called “morning-after pills.” Mechanism Primarily inhibit ovulation May also prevent fertilization Dosage (classical regimen) Taken within 72 hours of unprotected sex Two doses are taken 12 hours apart Effectiveness Prevent approximately 75% of expected pregnancies (d) Once-a-Month Pills: These contain a long-acting estrogen combined with a short-acting progesterone, taken once monthly. (e) Male Pill: Contains gossypol, a derivative of cottonseed oil.

Acts by reducing sperm production and count Adverse Effects of Oral Contraceptives 1. Myocardial infarction 2. Thromboembolic events 3. Breast cancer (risk association context-dependent) 4. Hyperglycemia 5. Hypertension 6. Jaundice 7. Weight gain 8. Nausea and vomitng Advantages 1. Easy oral administration 2. Highly effective (near 100% with correct use) Disadvantages 1. May reduce breast milk 2. Associated with side effects and contraindications 3. Delay in return to fertility in some cases Depot Formulations (a) Injectable Contraceptives Drugs used: DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate), NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate) Administered once every 3 months Mechanism Inhibits ovulation Thickens cervical mucus Does not affect existing pregnancy Advantages 1. Highly effective 2. Long-acting (3 months per dose) 3. No estrogen-related side effects 4. Does not interfere with sexual activity Disadvantages 1. Weight gain 2. Headache, breast tenderness, mood changes 3. Nausea and hair loss in some women 4. No protection against STDs/HIV Contraindications 1. Breast or genital cancer 2. Unexplained vaginal bleeding (b) Subdermal Implants

Example: Norplant (contains levonorgestrel) Implanted under the skin of the upper arm Provides contraception for up to 5 years Mechanism Thickens cervical mucus Suppresses ovulation (partially over time) Disadvantages Irregular menstrual bleeding Requires minor surgical procedure for insertion and removal (c) Vaginal Rings 1. Contain hormones (e.g., levonorgestrel) 2. Hormones are absorbed through the vaginal mucosa 3. Bypass the digestive system and liver 4. Effective at lower doses 5. Post-Conceptional Methods 6. Menstrual regulation 7. Menstrual induction Miscellaneous Methods (a) Behavioral Methods 1. Abstinence 2. Coitus interruptus (withdrawal method) 3. Safe period method (avoid intercourse during days 9–14) (b) Natural Methods 1. Basal body temperature method 2. Cervical mucus method PERMANENT METHODS (STERILIZATION ) Sterilization is a permanent method of contraception for both males and females. Advantages 1. One-time procedure 2. No need for ongoing motivation 3. Cost-effective 4. Low complication rate when performed properly Male Sterilization (Vasectomy): A safe, simple, and quick surgical procedure for permanent contraception in men. Procedure 1. A small segment (~1 cm) of the vas deferens is removed 2. Ends are ligated and sealed

Complications 1. Hematoma and infection 2. Sperm granuloma 3. Rare spontaneous recanalization 4. Psychological concerns (rare) Female Sterilization (Tubectomy): A permanent contraceptive method for women, usually performed under local anesthesia. Methods 1. Laparoscopy Performed using a laparoscope Fallopian tubes are occluded using rings Advantages 1. Short operation time 2. Short hospital stay 3. Minimal scarring 2. Mini-Laparotomy Small abdominal incision Simple, safe, and effective procedure Fewer complication

title: Inventory Control Inventory Management
subject: Pharmacy Practice
text: INVENTORY CONTROL  In community pharmacies, pharmacists procure medicines from licensed authorized wholesalers or distributors and stock them adequately and dispense.  The whole activity looks very simple and straightforward.  Procurement of medicines from the suppliers depends upon o the sales/demand of a particular medicine o the decision of the pharmacist/person in charge of ordering, discounts received from the manufacturer and wholesaler.  Procurement involves the selection of medicines, assessing the quantity required, assessing the availability of sufficient funds, selecting the suppliers, obtaining the best deals and services, placing the orders, verifying the stocks ordered and actual stocks received, taking them into the stocks, making the payments to the suppliers.  Thus, credit and inventory control requires knowledge and skill in assessing the market demand, period of discount, distance between the wholesaler and retailer, supply policies of wholesaler, buying capacity, and transport facilities.  Thus, inventory control is an art and science.  An effective procurement process ensures the availability of all the medicines in the right quantities at reasonable prices at all the times.  This will ensure better cash rotation, excellent customer service, and improved professional relationship with the suppliers, fair returns on investments, and future growth of the business.  Thus, it is very important to understand the art of inventory control of medicines i

The objectives of inventory control are: To ensure uninterrupted production: To maintain sufficient inventory so as to avoid out of stock situation which leads to customer dissatisfaction loss of revenue and increase in cost investment. To avoid overstocking: Only the required quantities of medicines will be stocked in the stores and there is no need to keep in excess, which will lead to blockage of money. To facilitate economical purchasing: With proper control of inventories the medicines can be advanced by inviting the tenders/quotations. To optimize manpower utilization: During stock period the number of workers can be reduced whereas in boom periods the man power can be increased, thus money can be saved. To reduce wastage and obsolescence: With proper planning wastage and surplus can be reduced. To prevent theft and pilferage: Having control over the inventories the theft of small but costly items can be checked. Functions of Inventory Control 1. Efficient utilization of resources Ensures proper use of men, machines, and materials. 2. Systematic assessment of material requirements Helps in accurate forecasting and planning of material needs. 3. Control of wastage and theft Reduces losses due to spoilage, damage, or pilferage. 4. Quick response to customer demand Enables supply of finished goods at short notice when demand arises. 5. Procurement at lowest cost and right time Ensures timely availability of materials at economical prices. 6. Maintaining minimum stock level

ABC analysis (Always Better Control)  ABC stands for Always Better Control  ABC analysis is based on the principle that: “All inventory items are not of equal importance.”  ABC analysis is a selective inventory control technique based on the annual consumption value of items. highlighting the need for continuous and focused control on important inventory items.  It helps in identifying the items that require strict managerial control and those that require simple control, thereby ensuring economical and efficient inventory management.  A small percentage of items accounts for a major share of inventory investment, while a large number of items account for a minor share of total value.  Annual inventory value is calculated as: Annual usage × Unit cost  It is a simple, effective, and widely used inventory control technique that helps in prioritizing inventory items based on their value.  By applying different levels of control to different categories, it ensures better utilization of capital, reduced losses, and improved efficiency, especially in hospital pharmacy and industrial inventory management. Need for ABC Analysis  To ensure better control of high-value items  To avoid over-investment of capital  To minimize storage and carrying costs  To prevent pilferage, theft, and losses  To improve decision-making for reordering Classification of Items under ABC Analysis According to ABC analysis, inventory items are classified into three categories based on their valu

75% of the budget, Require strict control to prevent pilferage and expiry losses drugs, Consume around 20% of the budget the total budget, Can be purchased in bulk. Control Characteristics a. Very strict control b. Frequent ordering (weekly or continuous review) c. No or very low safety stock d. Close supervision and follow-up e. Accurate record keeping a. Moderate control b. Periodic review c. Low safety stock d. Ordering once in 2–3 months e. Routine supervision a. Loose control b. High safety stock c. Bulk ordering d. Follow-up only in exceptional cases e. Ordering once in six months or annually Advantages of ABC Analysis 1. Ensures effective control over costly items 2. Helps in optimum utilization of financial resources 3. Reduces inventory carrying and storage costs 4. Facilitates scientific and systematic inventory control 5. Improves efficiency of inventory planning and purchasing 6. Helps management focus on critical items Disadvantages of ABC Analysis 1. B and C category items may get neglected 2. Risk of overstocking or pilferage in C category items 3. Does not consider criticality of items 4. Requires accurate and updated cost data 5. Not suitable when usage pattern fluctuates frequently VED (Vital–Essential–Desirable) Analysis  VED analysis is an inventory control technique based on the criticality or importance of items, rather than their cost.  The basic principle of VED analysis is: “The importance of an item is more significant than its cost.”  This method

o Automobile and engineering industries o Maintenance and spare parts management Classification under VED Analysis Based on usage and importance, items are classified into three categories: Vital (V) Items Essential (E) Items Desirable (D) Items a. Most critical and life- saving items b. Non-availability may cause: a. Loss of life (healthcare) b. Complete stoppage of production for several days (industry) c. Must always be available in stock a. Necessary for effective functioning b. Short-term non-availability may: a. Worsen the condition b. Interrupt production for a few hours a. Useful but not critical b. Non-availability does not seriously affect performance or patient outcome Characteristics a. No stock-out permitted b. High safety stock c. Strict control and continuous monitoring d. Emergency procurement if required a. Moderate safety stock b. Periodic review c. Controlled inventory management a. Low priority b. Minimal control c. Can tolerate stock-outs for a limited period Examples in Healthcare: 1) Atropine injection (pesticide poisoning) 2) Adrenaline injection 3) Insulin 4) Anti-snake venom 1) Proton pump inhibitors (Omeprazole, Pantoprazole) for acid peptic disease 2) Antibiotics for common infections 3) Antihypertensive drugs 1) B-complex vitamins 2) Multivitamin supplements 3) Tonics and nutritional supplements Healthcare Example of VED Analysis  In the healthcare sector, medicines are classified based on their therapeutic importance and ability to save life, ir

Industrial Example of VED Analysis In pharmaceutical products:  Disprin tablets – High demand → Vital  Anacin tablets – Moderate demand → Essential  APC tablets – Low demand → Desirable Advantages of VED Analysis 1. Ensures continuous availability of critical items 2. Prevents life-threatening situations due to stock-outs 3. Improves patient care and safety 4. Helps in priority-based inventory management 5. Simple and easy to implement Limitations of VED Analysis 1. Does not consider cost of items 2. May result in high inventory investment 3. Subjective classification 4. Requires expert judgement 5. Not suitable when budget constraints are strict Combination of ABC and VED Analysis: This combined approach ensures cost control along with criticality control. For effective inventory control, ABC and VED analyses are often combined , it provides a comprehensive and efficient inventory management system. AV items → Highest priority / BV items → Medium priority / CV items → Lowest priority Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) Method  Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) is one of the most widely used inventory control techniques in pharmacy practice.  EOQ is defined as the quantity of inventory that minimizes the total cost, which includes ordering (procurement) cost and carrying (holding) cost, without affecting demand and supply.  It helps in determining the optimum quantity of a medicine that should be ordered at one time so that the total inventory cost is minimized.  When the demand

Another commonly used formula to determine EOQ is: EOQ = ඨ 2 × ( Annual usage in units) × ( Order cost ) Annual carrying cost per unit Costs Involved in EOQ: EOQ is based on two major costs: 1) Procuring (Ordering) Cost: Procuring cost includes all expenses involved in placing and receiving an order, such as: a. Communication expenses b. Receiving quotations c. Advertising or media costs d. Preparation and processing of purchase orders e. Follow-up and expediting purchase orders f. Receiving and inspection of goods g. Marking, stocking, and record maintenance h. Processing supplier invoices.  Procuring cost decreases as order quantity increases, because fewer orders are placed. 2. Carrying (Holding) Cost: Carrying cost includes expenses incurred while storing inventory, such as: a. Storage and warehousing costs b. Insurance charges c. Interest on capital investment d. Deterioration, damage, and obsolescence e. Record keeping and handling costs f. Taxes and security costs  Carrying cost increases as order quantity increases, because more inventory is held for longer periods.  Carrying cost reduces when order size decreases, but frequent ordering increases procurement cost. The EOQ model provides a level of inventory at which the total cost is minimum. Total Inventory Cost = Procurement Cost + Carrying Cost Graphical representation of EOQ method

Applications of EOQ 1. EOQ helps in calculating the most economical order size. 2. It shows how inventory levels should change with an increase in sales. 3. If sales increase by 20%, inventory increases approximately by the square root of 20. 4. Useful for planning purchasing schedules in pharmacy stores and hospitals. Advantages of EOQ a. Minimizes total inventory cost b. Balances ordering and holding costs c. Prevents stock-outs d. Helps maintain optimal inventory levels e. Provides a systematic approach to inventory management. Limitations of EOQ a. Assumes constant demand and stable consumption pattern b. Assumes prices remain constant c. Assumes unlimited storage space d. Ordering and carrying costs may not be accurately measurable e. Not suitable for irregular or seasonal demand f. Does not consider quantity discounts g. Not time-phased (assumes immediate replenishment) h. EOQ may not match minimum supplier order quantities i. Requires accurate and updated stock records j. Less effective when multiple items must be ordered simultaneously Lead time Lead time is the total time taken from ordering the materials to receiving them into inventory. or Lead time is defined as the time interval between placing an order with the supplier and the actual receipt of the ordered stock in the pharmacy or store.  It plays a crucial role in determining order quantity, re-order level, and safety stock.  Lead time is a critical factor in inventory control. 4. Availability of discounts and credit facilities 5. Approval procedures 2. Delivery Time: Delivery time is the time taken by the supplier from receipt of the order to dispatch and transport of goods. Activities involved: 1. Order processing 2. Separation and picking of items 3. Billing and documentation 4. Packing 5. Selection of transport method Factors affecting delivery time: 1. Non-availability of ordered stock 2. Inadequate clerical staff 3. Distance from supplier 4. Transportation delays 3. Receiving Time: Receiving time is the time taken by the pharmacy to receive the dispatched stocks. Factors affecting receiving time: 1. Efficiency of transport system 2. Location of pharmacy (urban vs rural) 3. Road and infrastructure facilities 4. Handling and unloading procedures Pharmacies located in rural or remote areas usually experience longer receiving time. Safety Stock / Buffer Stock Safety stock refers to the extra quantity of inventory kept as a buffer to meet unexpected increases in demand or delays in supply. It acts as a protective cushion to ensure uninterrupted operations and customer service. or Safety stock is the minimum additional quantity of materials maintained to prevent stock-out due to unforeseen fluctuations in demand or supply.  Safety stock plays a vital role in inventory management by acting as a buffer against uncertainty.  Maintaining an optimum level of safety stock helps organizations balance between avoiding stock-outs and minimizing carrying co

5. Loss of goodwill and revenue Optimal Level of Safety Stock  Low safety stock  Frequent stock-outs  High opportunity cost  Production interruptions  High safety stock  Increased carrying and storage costs  Capital blockage  Risk of obsolescence and expiry Hence, optimum safety stock level must be maintained. Advantages of Safety Stock 1. Prevents zero-stock situations 2. Compensates for forecasting errors 3. Ensures uninterrupted supply 4. Improves customer service 5. Reduces emergency purchasing Disadvantages of Safety Stock 1. Increases storage and carrying costs 2. Blocks working capital 3. Does not account for extreme or unusual delivery delays 4. Requires periodic review of reorder level 5. Risk of wastage or expiry Re-Order Quantity Level (Re-Order Point)  The re-order quantity level, also called the re-order point, is the inventory level at which a fresh order for materials should be placed. It ensures that new stock arrives before the existing stock is exhausted, thereby preventing stock-out situations. or  Re-order level is the level of inventory at which a new purchase order is initiated to replenish stock.  The re-order quantity level is a critical element of inventory control that helps determine the right time to place an order.  By considering lead time, usage rate, and safety stock, organizations can maintain continuous availability of materials while avoiding overstocking and unnecessary costs. Concept of Re-Order Level  Re-order point is genera

Graphical Representation  Maximum stock level – Upper limit of inventory  Re-order point – Level at which new order is placed  Minimum stock level – Lower limit of inventory  Buffer / safety stock – Extra stock to prevent stock-out As stock decreases with time, once it reaches the re-order point, a new order is placed so that stock does not fall below the minimum level. Minimum Stock Level  The minimum stock level is the quantity that must be maintained at all times.  If inventory falls below this level: Customer demand cannot be met  Factors affecting minimum stock level: 1. Lead time: Time taken to process and receive the order. 2. Rate of consumption: Average usage of material. 3. Nature of materials  Regular-use items → Minimum stock required  Special-order items → Minimum stock may not be required Maximum Stock Level  The maximum stock level is the upper limit of inventory beyond which stock should not be held.  Problems of exceeding maximum level: a. Overstocking b. Increased material cost c. Blockage of working capital d. Need for more storage space e. Higher risk of wastage, expiry, and obsolescence Importance of Re-Order Level  Prevents stock-out situations  Ensures uninterrupted production or service  Helps maintain optimum inventory levels  Reduces emergency purchasing  Improves inventory planning

Bin Card System  Bin Card System is a method of inventory control in which a separate card is maintained for each item, showing the details of receipts, issues, and balance of stock on a day-to-day basis.  The Bin Card System is one of the simplest and most reliable methods of inventory control.  The bin card is usually kept near or attached to the storage bin or shelf containing the product, allowing easy and quick access to stock information.  The Bin Card System is a basic yet effective inventory control method that provides real- time information on stock levels.  When maintained properly and updated daily, it helps pharmacists ensure efficient stock management, FIFO compliance, and reduced wastage, making it an essential tool in pharmacy inventory management. Contents of a Bin Card: A bin card contains the following information: 1) Name of the product 2) Manufacturer’s name 3) Batch number 4) Date of supply 5) Expiry date 6) Unit price 7) Quantity received 8) Quantity issued / sold daily 9) Balance stock after each transaction 10) Signature of the person making the entry Working of Bin Card System 1. A separate bin card is prepared for every product. 2. Whenever stock is received, the quantity is entered in the bin card. 3. When stock is issued or sold, the quantity is deducted and the balance is updated. 4. Entries are made on a daily basis. 5. The updated balance shows the current stock position at any time. 6. Older stock is issued first by following the First-In

4. Facilitates FIFO method, reducing expiry losses 5. Assists in timely re-ordering 6. Useful for physical stock verification 7. Reduces chances of pilferage and error Limitations of Bin Card System 1. Requires regular and careful updating 2. Time-consuming when the number of items is large 3. Does not show the monetary value of stock 4. Chances of error if entries are not made immediately 5. Needs supervision to maintain accuracy Perpetual Inventory Control Method  Perpetual inventory control is a system of inventory management in which the stock balance of each item is continuously updated and can be obtained on any day from stock records. Or  It is defined as a system in which the quantity and value of inventory items can be known at any time from stock records without waiting for a physical stock-taking at the end of a period.  In this method, every receipt, issue, purchase, and consumption of materials is recorded immediately in inventory records, thereby providing a continuous (perpetual) record of stock position  The Perpetual Inventory Control Method is one of the most effective and accurate systems of inventory control.  The Perpetual Inventory Control Method is a reliable and systematic approach that provides continuous information about inventory levels.  With regular updating and computer support, it ensures accurate stock control, reduced losses, and efficient management, making it highly suitable for hospital pharmacies and industrial inventory systems. 6. Use of computers: Computerized inventory systems simplify record-keeping and provide real-time stock information. Procedure of Perpetual Inventory Control 1. Recording of all receipts and issues in bin cards / stock cards 2. Maintenance of stores ledger 3. Continuous update of stock balances 4. Periodic physical stock verification 5. Comparison of physical stock with recorded stock 6. Adjustment of discrepancies Advantages of Perpetual Inventory Control 1. Provides accurate and up-to-date stock information 2. Helps in avoiding stock-outs and over-stocking 3. Facilitates better planning and timely reordering 4. Detects pilferage, theft, and wastage 5. Eliminates the need for year-end stock taking 6. Supports efficient budget and purchase control 7. Improves accounting accuracy Disadvantages of Perpetual Inventory Control 1. Requires skilled manpower 2. Involves higher administrative cost 3. Continuous record-keeping can be time-consuming 4. Errors may occur if entries are not updated properly 5. Needs effective supervision and discipline Physical Inventory  Physical inventory refers to the actual physical verification and counting of stock available in the store or pharmacy at regular intervals such as weekly, monthly, or quarterly. It involves comparing the physically available stock with the recorded stock to ensure accuracy. or  Physical inventory is the method of inventory control in which the actual stock is physically counted at regular intervals to determine the co

5. Corrective action: Discrepancies due to pilferage, spoilage, breakage, or errors are corrected. Importance of Physical Inventory 1. Helps in identifying non-moving and dead stock 2. Enables replacement or return of slow-moving stock to suppliers 3. Prevents expiry-related losses 4. Detects pilferage and spoilage 5. Ensures accuracy of inventory records 6. Improves stock planning and purchasing decisions Advantages of Physical Inventory 1. Simple and easy to understand 2. Accurate method of stock verification 3. Helps in controlling theft and wastage 4. Reduces financial losses due to expiry 5. Improves coordination between supplier and retailer 6. Provides actual stock position Limitations of Physical Inventory 1. Time-consuming process 2. May interrupt routine pharmacy operations 3. Not suitable for large inventories if done frequently 4. Errors may occur during manual counting Open-to-Buy (OTB) Budget System  Open-to-Buy budget system is a method of inventory control in which a fixed amount is allocated for purchasing stock during a specific period, and purchases are made only within the remaining available budget.  The system is based on the principle that: Purchases should be made only after considering available budget, existing stock, and expected sales.  The Open-to-Buy (OTB) Budget System is an inventory control and financial planning method commonly used in hospital pharmacies.  It helps in controlling purchases by ensuring that inventory is bought within the

2. Allocation of pharmacy budget: The total pharmacy budget is divided into monthly or quarterly limits. 3. Ordering of stock: Based on sales requirements and consumption trends, the pharmacy manager places orders. 4. Debit of purchases: The value of purchased medicines is debited from the allocated budget. 5. Monitoring of balance: The remaining open-to-buy amount is continuously monitored. 6. Control of purchases: Purchases are restricted once the budget limit is reached. Advantages of Open-to-Buy Budget System 1. Prevents over-stocking 2. Reduces stock-out situations 3. Ensures optimum utilization of funds 4. Helps in purchase planning and control 5. Avoids unwanted stock accumulation 6. Improves coordination between sales and purchases 7. Facilitates budget monitoring and accountability Limitations of Open-to-Buy Budget System 1. Depends heavily on accurate sales forecasting 2. Not suitable during sudden emergencies 3. Requires continuous monitoring 4. May restrict purchase of unexpectedly required items 5.
